title: Oliver's Oreos
summary: Bacon-wrapped smoked Oreos from Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop. Sweet, salty, smoky — the cookie goes soft and cake-like inside crisp bacon.
story: Named for Oliver, Kelly's grandson, and the featured treat at Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop.

items: 1 pack Oreo cookies (regular, not Double Stuf)

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap each Oreo in one slice of bacon, overlapping the seam underneath. Pin with a toothpick.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.body: Dust each one lightly with brown sugar.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F over apple or cherry wood for 60–90 minutes, until the bacon is crisp and browned.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes — the filling comes out molten. Pull the toothpicks before serving.

title: Brooklyn's Brownies
finish: Edges set, center just barely jiggles
summary: Smoked skillet brownies from Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop. Fudgy dark chocolate loaded with walnuts and pecans, kissed with cherry wood smoke.
story: Named for Brooklyn, Kelly's granddaughter — Sissy herself — and baked for the sweet shop.

items: 8 oz semi-sweet chocolate chips (about 1 1/3 cups), plus 1/2 cup more for the top
Flaky sea salt, for the top (optional)

steps.title: Melt
steps.body: Melt the butter and 8 oz chocolate together; cool 5 minutes.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk in both sugars, then the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.

steps.title: Fold
steps.body: Fold in the flour, cocoa, and salt just until combined. Fold in the extra 1/2 cup chips, the walnuts, and the pecans.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pour into a buttered 10-inch cast iron skillet. Smoke at 325°F over cherry or apple wood for 35–45 minutes, until the edges are set and the center just barely jiggles.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes — the center firms up as it cools. Sprinkle flaky salt, cut, and serve.

title: Smoked Deviled Eggs
summary: Real smoked deviled eggs — the eggs go on the smoker raw in the shell and come off hard-boiled with smoke all the way through.
story: No shortcuts here: the eggs cook right on the smoker in their shells, so the smoke gets into the egg itself, not just the filling. Kelly likes his deviled eggs just a touch sweet — enough to taste it, never enough to argue with the smoke.
school: Smoke the eggs in the shell — the shell takes the smoke and the egg takes the flavor. An ice bath right off the smoker is what makes them peel clean.

items: Crumbled crispy bacon or thin jalapeño slices, for the top (optional)

steps.title: Fire up
steps.body: Get the smoker to 225°F with apple or cherry wood rolling thin and blue.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Set the eggs right on the grate, in the shell. Smoke 2 hours, turning them once at the hour mark.

steps.title: Ice bath
steps.body: Drop the eggs straight into an ice bath for 15 minutes — that's what makes them peel clean.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Peel, halve lengthwise, and pop the yolks into a bowl. Mash with the mayo, mustard, relish, sugar, vinegar, salt, and pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Spoon or pipe the filling back into the whites. Dust with smoked paprika and top with bacon or jalapeño if you're feeling it.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Chill at least 30 minutes before serving — they're better cold.

title: Fair-Style Smoked Turkey Legs
finish: 175°F internal, meat pulling back from the bone
summary: Big, juicy, smoky turkey legs just like the state fair — brined overnight, rubbed down, and smoked till tender.
story: Everybody remembers their first fair turkey leg — the size of it, the smoky smell, eating it walking around with juice running down your arm. These are that leg. An overnight salt-and-brown-sugar brine keeps them juicy, a paprika rub builds the crust, and 275°F of hickory or pecan smoke does the rest. Take them to 175°F so the meat pulls back from the bone and eats tender, not tough.

items: 1 tsp cayenne, optional for a little kick

steps.title: Brine overnight
steps.body: Stir the water, salt, brown sugar, and the Prague Powder #1 (if using) until dissolved. Submerge the legs and brine in the fridge 8 to 12 hours, or overnight.

steps.title: Rinse and rub
steps.body: Pull the legs out, rinse, and pat dry. Let them sit out 30 minutes to take the chill off. Mix the rub ingredients and coat the legs all over.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 3 to 4 hours, until the meat hits 175°F internal and pulls back from the bone a little. If they're getting dark, wrap in foil for the last hour.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before serving.

proTips: The fair legs get that pink, ham-like color from cure. If you want it, stir 2 1/2 tsp Prague Powder #1 (pink curing salt — that’s Cure #1, not Cure #2) into the brine with the salt and sugar. That’s the measured amount for 4 legs in a gallon of brine, so measure it — don’t eyeball cure. Totally optional; still great without it.

title: Smoked Crawfish Bowl
finish: Crawfish heated through, everything drizzled with seasoned butter
summary: Frozen crawfish tails sautéed in spicy butter, piled over rice with smoked sausage, corn, and potatoes. No purging, no giant pot.
story: Most folks aren't going to purge live crawfish — they'll grab the frozen tail meat at Walmart, and that's just fine. This bowl brings the whole boil to the table without the work: smoky sausage from the pit, sweet corn, tender potatoes, and crawfish tails warmed through in Cajun-spiced butter, all over rice. If you do get your hands on live ones, boil them 3 to 5 minutes till red and soak them off the heat 15 to 20 minutes, then pile everything together.

items: 2 lbs frozen crawfish tails, thawed and drained
1 lb andouille sausage (or kielbasa), cut in 2-inch pieces
3 ears corn, cut in 2-inch rounds (or 2 cups frozen)
2 Tbsp Cajun seasoning (like Zatarain's or Slap Ya Mama), divided

steps.title: Smoke the sausage
steps.body: Smoke the sausage at 250°F for 1 hour. Skip this if it's already smoked.

steps.title: Boil the potatoes and corn
steps.body: Boil the potatoes 12 minutes, add the corn for the last 5. Drain.

steps.title: Sauté the crawfish
steps.body: Melt the butter with the garlic and 1 Tbsp Cajun seasoning. Add the crawfish tails and sauté 3 to 4 minutes, just until heated through — don't overcook them.

steps.title: Build the bowls
steps.body: Rice first, then sausage, potatoes, corn, and crawfish. Spoon the seasoned butter from the pan over everything. Squeeze of lemon on top. Pass the hot sauce at the table for whoever wants the extra kick.

proTips: If you get live crawfish, boil them 3 to 5 minutes until red, then soak off the heat 15 to 20 minutes before piling everything together.
Thawed tails cook fast — 3 to 4 minutes is plenty. Any longer and they go rubbery.

title: Smoked Crawfish Hand Pies
summary: Flaky, golden hand pies stuffed with Cajun-spiced crawfish tails. Fair food you can hold in one hand.
story: Crawfish pies are Louisiana fair food at heart, and Mississippi does them proud too. The filling is the Cajun trinity — onion, bell pepper, celery — bound with a quick roux and loaded with crawfish tails, then folded into pie crust and baked golden. Smoke the filling first if you want the pit in every bite.

items: 1 lb frozen crawfish tails, thawed, drained, and chopped

steps.title: Cook the trinity
steps.body: Melt the butter and cook the onion, bell pepper, and celery 5 minutes. Add the garlic, 1 minute more.

steps.title: Make it creamy
steps.body: Stir in the flour and cook 1 minute. Pour in the broth and stir until thick.

steps.title: Add the crawfish
steps.body: Fold in the crawfish and Cajun seasoning. Cook 2 to 3 minutes, then cool 10 minutes.

steps.title: Cut the rounds
steps.body: Unroll the crusts and cut 4 rounds from each, about 5 inches — a small bowl works as a guide.

steps.title: Fill and crimp
steps.body: Spoon filling onto half of each round. Brush the edges with beaten egg, fold over, and crimp with a fork.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Brush the tops with egg and cut a small vent in each. Bake at 400°F for 20 to 25 minutes, until deep golden.

proTips: Pit twist: smoke the filling in a pan at 250°F for 30 minutes before filling the pies.
Cool the filling before you fill — hot filling melts the crust and makes it soggy.

title: Smoked Chicken Pot Pie
finish: Deep golden, filling bubbling at the vents
summary: Classic chicken pot pie, but the chicken comes off the smoker first — that's the whole difference.
story: Chicken pot pie is pure comfort, and the smoker makes it better without making it fussy. Smoke the bird at 275°F, shred it into a creamy filling with potatoes, carrots, peas, and thyme, and bake it under a golden crust. Kelly's version adds diced potatoes — they soak up the gravy and make every slice eat like a meal.

items: 3 cups smoked chicken, shredded or diced
2 medium potatoes, peeled and diced small

steps.title: Smoke the chicken
steps.body: If your chicken isn't smoked yet: smoke at 275°F until 165°F inside, about 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Leftover smoked chicken works perfect here.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables
steps.body: Melt the butter and cook the onion, carrots, celery, and potatoes 8 to 10 minutes, until the potatoes are just tender.

steps.title: Make the gravy
steps.body: Stir in the flour and cook 2 minutes. Whisk in the broth and milk and simmer until thick.

steps.title: Fill it out
steps.body: Fold in the chicken, peas, thyme, salt, and pepper.

steps.title: Assemble
steps.body: Line a pie dish with one crust, fill it, and lay the second crust on top. Crimp the edges, cut vents, and brush with beaten egg.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Bake at 400°F for 30 to 35 minutes, until deep golden. Rest 10 minutes before cutting.

proTips: Dice the potatoes small so they cook through — big chunks stay crunchy.
Rest the full 10 minutes. Cut it hot and the filling runs everywhere.

title: Smoked Baja Fish Tacos
summary: Flaky smoked cod in warm corn tortillas with crunchy cabbage slaw and chipotle-lime crema. Baja beach food, pit-style.
story: Baja fish tacos are usually fried, but the smoker does something better — a whisper of alder or apple smoke that the slaw and crema were made for. Cod or tilapia, a simple chili-cumin rub, 25 to 30 minutes at 225°F, then flaked into warm corn tortillas. The chipotle-lime crema brings the heat and the lime brings it all home.

steps.title: Season the fish
steps.body: Rub the fish with olive oil, chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, salt, and pepper.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 225°F for 25 to 30 minutes, until the fish flakes easily and hits 145°F inside.

steps.title: Mix the slaw and crema
steps.body: While the fish smokes, toss the slaw ingredients together and stir up the crema.

steps.title: Warm the tortillas
steps.body: Warm the tortillas on the grill or in a dry skillet.

steps.title: Build the tacos
steps.body: Flake the fish into the tortillas, pile on the slaw, and drizzle with crema. Lime wedge and cilantro on top.

proTips: Don't over-smoke it — 30 minutes is plenty. Fish takes on smoke fast.
Warm tortillas are non-negotiable. Cold tortillas crack and the whole thing falls apart.

title: Candy Apple Pork Belly
summary: Pork belly strips smoked low, braised tender in apple juice, then dunked in a sticky candy-apple glaze. Inspired by Malcom Reed's HowToBBQRight video.
story: Sweet, sticky, and gone in minutes. Thick pork belly strips get a honey-mustard slather and a generous coat of apple rub, then smoke low until the bark sets. A braise in apple juice takes them the rest of the way to tender, and the finish is pure candy apple — melted apple jelly and sweet and sour sauce, dunked on a skewer and set back on the pit. This one started as Malcolm Reed's HowToBBQRight video, and it earned its spot here.

items: 1/4 cup apple rub (or your favorite sweet pork rub)

steps.title: Fire the smoker
steps.body: Get your smoker running at 250°F, indirect, with apple wood.

steps.title: Cut the belly
steps.body: Cut the pork belly in half, then cut each half into thirds — you want strips about 2 inches wide.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Slather every strip with honey mustard, then season generous with the apple rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Lay the strips on the smoker and cook about 3 hours, until they hit around 170°F inside and the bark is set.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Move the strips into an aluminum half pan, pour in the apple juice, cover tight with foil, and cook another hour — until 200–205°F and a probe slides in easy.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body: Melt the apple jelly and sweet and sour sauce together in a microwave-safe bowl, 3–5 minutes, stirring now and then.

steps.title: Dunk and set
steps.body: Pull the strips out of the pan onto a wire rack. Stick a skewer in each one, dunk it in the glaze, dust a little more rub on top, and put them back on the pit about 5 minutes to set the glaze.

proTips: Don't skip the rest — give them 10 minutes off the heat before serving so that glaze sets up sticky instead of sliding off.
Cut the strips even. A skinny strip finishes way before a fat one and there's no fixing that on the pit.

title: Smoked Jack-o'-Lantern Stuffed Peppers
finish: Peppers tender, cheese melted and golden
summary: Orange bell peppers carved like jack-o'-lanterns, stuffed with sausage (or beef) and rice, finished on the pit.
story: The kids carve the faces and the smoker does the rest. Big orange bell peppers get the jack-o'-lantern treatment, then get stuffed full of browned smoked sausage or ground beef, rice, and tomatoes under a blanket of melted cheese. An hour or so on the pit and you've got the centerpiece of the Halloween table — and yes, they taste as good as they look.

items: 1 Tbsp of your favorite BBQ rub
1 lb smoked sausage (kielbasa works) or ground beef, diced or crumbled
1 can (10 oz) diced tomatoes with green chiles, drained
2 cups shredded cheddar or pepper jack

steps.title: Carve the peppers
steps.body: Cut the tops off the peppers and scoop out the seeds and membranes. Carve a jack-o'-lantern face into each one with a small sharp knife — keep the cuts simple so the pepper holds together.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.body: Brown the sausage (or ground beef) and onion in a skillet over medium-high heat. Stir in the cooked rice, drained tomatoes, half the cheese, and the BBQ rub.

steps.title: Stuff them
steps.body: Pack each pepper full of filling and top with the remaining cheese.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the peppers are tender and the cheese is melted and golden.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes before serving so the filling sets up.

proTips: Stand the peppers in a muffin tin or crimped foil rings so they don't tip over on the grate.
Don't carve the faces too deep or too big — thin walls collapse in the heat.
Use ground beef instead of sausage if you like — Kelly makes it with beef.

title: Bacon Mummy Jalapeño Poppers
summary: Jalapeño poppers wrapped in bacon like mummy bandages, with googly candy eyes. The Halloween appetizer that disappears first.
story: Every Halloween spread needs something the kids can grab with one hand. Cream cheese and cheddar stuffed into jalapeños, wrapped up in bacon strips like little mummies, and smoked low until the bacon crisps. The candy eyes go on after — that's what makes the whole tray look alive.

steps.title: Prep the peppers
steps.body: Cut the jalapeños in half lengthwise and scoop out the seeds and membranes. Wear gloves — your hands will thank you.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.body: Stir the cream cheese, cheddar, and garlic powder together until smooth.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Fill each jalapeño half generously with the cheese mixture.

steps.title: Wrap like a mummy
steps.body: Wrap each popper with a strip of bacon, crisscrossing it like mummy bandages. Leave a little gap near the top for the face.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for 1.5 to 2 hours, until the bacon is crisped and the cheese is bubbly.

steps.title: Add the eyes
steps.body: Let them cool a couple minutes, then press two candy eyes into the cheese in the face gap of each mummy.

proTips: Thin bacon crisps better than thick cut — thick bacon stays chewy at 250°F.
Put the eyes on after the smoke, not before. They melt into blobs in the heat.

title: Smoked Pumpkin Pie
wood: Apple or pecan (light — easy on the smoke)
summary: Classic pumpkin pie baked on the smoker with a whisper of apple or pecan smoke. Fall in a crust.
story: The smoker isn't just for meat — it bakes a fine pie. Same pumpkin pie you grew up with, but the crust picks up the faintest kiss of apple or pecan smoke on its way through. Keep the smoke light; this one is about the pie, not the pit.

steps.title: Heat the smoker
steps.body: Get the smoker to 350°F, indirect, with a light wood like apple or pecan. Go easy — a little smoke goes a long way on dessert.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.body: Whisk the pumpkin, evaporated milk, eggs, brown sugar, pumpkin pie spice, and salt until completely smooth.

steps.title: Fill the crust
steps.body: Pour the filling into the pie crust.

steps.title: Smoke-bake
steps.body: Bake on the smoker at 350°F for 50 to 60 minutes, until the edges are set and the center barely jiggles when you nudge the pan.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool at least 2 hours so the filling sets. Serve with whipped cream.

proTips: Light wood and a clean fire — heavy smoke turns the pie bitter.
That little jiggle in the center is right. It sets as it cools; an overbaked pie cracks.
